blocks.text: 1. OBJECTIVE

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and dose-response of OCU400 drug product in mouse model RhoP23H following a single subretinal administration of different doses. This study was a proof-of-concept efficacy study of the ability for OCU400 to rescue and potentially reverse the retinal degeneration phenotypes in this model intended to support future clinical studies.
2. BACKGROUND

OCU400 is an adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (AAV5)-based vector containing the human NR2E3 gene intended for the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases related to mutations in the NR2E3 and other retinal genes. The product is intended to be administered via a single subretinal dose.
2.1. Justification of the Animal Model Selected and Relevance to the Human Population
container_path: 2.1. Justification of the Animal Model Selected and Relevance to the Human Population

blocks.text:
Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of heterogeneous, pleiotropic inherited retinal diseases that that affects one in every 1000-4000 individuals. These diseases include syndromic and nonsyndromic forms.1-6 RP is the most common cause of inherited visual loss. Currently, there is no cure for RP and over 40% of RP cannot be genetically diagnosed. RP is heterogeneous and varies greatly in age of onset, rate of progression, and even genetic etiology, yet a common pathology of photoreceptor (PR) cell degeneration develops. Our lab and others have shown that phenotypic outcome results from a mutational load on a biological system that includes the primary mutation and other factors such as modifier alleles impacting the normal homeostatic state.7-18 As these modifier alleles are master regulators of development and maintenance of homeostasis in the retina, they can be more effective therapeutic agents, and especially beneficial in cases where the primary mutation cannot be identified.

RP is the most common cause of inherited blindness. Over 200 mutations in approximately 100 genes are known to cause RP, and while there are several gene replacement clinical trials in progress, they are only for a few known RP genes and rely on identifying the primary mutation, which is not possible for approximately 40% of all RP patients.6,11,19-27 Additionally, severity and progression of RP disease is greatly impacted by the genetic background in which the mutation is present. Furthermore, while RP is a rare disease, there are currently more than 150 known mutations in the rhodopsin (Rho) gene that account for approximately 40% of all autosomal dominant forms of RP and the RhoP23H mutation accounts for approximately 10% of RHO related adRP in the US (https://sph.uth.edu/Retnet).28 Dominant rhodopsin mutations create a toxic environment. The RhoP23H mutation creates a misfolded protein that is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Work by others showed that Ire1 signaling upregulates ER chaperones that can promote RhoP23H rhodopsin exit by partially correcting the misfolded protein.29-31 Our recent studies show that NR2E3 regulates this signaling pathway by modulating expression of Ire1.

The RhoP23H mouse is a model for the human adRP and recapitulates the human retinal disease. RhoP23H mice exhibit rapid retinal degeneration apparent at 14 days with heterozygous mice

blocks.text: 5.1.2. Justification of Number of Animals

The number of animals used in this study is the minimum necessary to satisfy scientific principles and/or regulatory requirements. To the knowledge of the Study Director and Sponsor, conduct of this study will result in no unnecessary duplication of existing data with regard to test species, test article, dose(s), route and duration of administration. Power calculation was conducted using G*Power 3.1 software analysis for estimating sample size required for each analysis and quantification described as indicated. Means and standard deviation defined by previously published studies, were used to provide 90% power and 30% difference at significant level of 0.05.

Based on power analysis and two decades of experience, we need minimum 5 biological replicates showing consistent data analysis to ensure statistical significance, scientific rigor, and demonstrate reproducibility of experiments. A minimum of N=5 animals/group were be dosed with test article and monitored for in-life measurements.

blocks.text: 5.2.1. Handling and Safety Procedures

Routine safety procedures for handling potentially toxic agents and viral vectors used in this study were followed to ensure the health and safety of personnel handling the test article or its formulations.
5.2.2. Assay

Records pertaining to the characterization of the Sponsor-supplied test and control articles, including their identity, composition, purity, stability, and method of synthesis, fabrication, and/or derivation will be maintained by the Sponsor. The Sponsor-provided Certificate of Analysis (COA) or equivalent and Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) for the provided test and control articles are provided in the Appendix.
5.2.3. Storage

The Sponsor-supplied test and control articles were stored in a freezer set to maintain -80℃ in the Sponsor-provided containers until use. Once a vial was thawed, test article was stored at 2- 8℃ and used within 24 hours of thawing. After 24 hours, thawed test article was not used for future administration. Vials were thawed on the day of dose administration.

6. METHODS
6.1. Animal Care
6.1.1. Food

Animals were fed commercially available guaranteed rodent diet (Purina Mills) that is stored in SERI's feed storage walk-in refrigerator unit to assure/prolong nutritional adequacy. Surplus rodent feed is also stored in the South storage room outside of the animal facility at SERI. Feed is monitored by milling date and managed on a first-in, first-out basis to ensure nutritional adequacy. Irradiated rodent diet is fed to all mice. A higher fat diet is provided to problem rodent breeders. Rodents are fed ad libitum in sanitized or sterilized feeders. When diets are transferred into covered plastic containers in individual animal rooms, the milling and expiration dates are placed on the containers and recorded in the notebook.
6.1.1.1. Food Consumption33
Average daily food intake:
~ 4-5 grams/mouse
Adjusted for body weight:
~ 5-6 grams of food per 30 grams body weight Average daily water intake: ~ 6 mL/mouse
Adjusted for body weight:
~ 8 mL of water per 30 grams body weight
6.1.2. Water
Water comes from municipal supply and is provided ad libitum by water bottles.
6.1.3. Animal Identification

Group-housed animals will be identified individually by ear punching (as necessary) and by cage card. Individually housed mice are identified primarily by cage card. All cage cards include the source of the animal, strain name of principal investigator, name and phone number of the responsible investigator, protocol number, and pertinent dates. Rodent breeding cage cards will have additional information pertaining to genetics, pedigree number, birth, and weaning dates.
6.1.4. Environmental Control

The environment in all individual animal rooms is monitored 24 hours a day for temperature and humidity using a computerized Siemens Environmental Monitoring System. Routine operating temperature specifications are 68-74°F for rabbits/rodents. The Siemens System is set to alarm if temperatures are outside these parameters. Temperature alarms will trigger the automated Siemens System to notify Plant Operations personnel via a modem/pager call out system. In addition, the animal facility staff monitors and records environmental parameters (HI/LO) temperature and humidity levels within each room on a daily basis during routine husbandry. The humidity levels are electronically monitored by the automated Siemens System and also by facilities personnel.
Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study in Rho Mice Report, v.02 Date of Report: 30 November 2021
6.1.5. Housing

SERI is an AAALAC accredited facility following all procedures and conditions outlined in The Guide and in compliance with federal regulations. Room ventilation rates are checked at least every three years by an outside HVAC contractor. There is an override switch in front of the experimental room that allows light to be turned on after hours. Light/dark cycles in all our animal rooms are controlled using automatic time clocks. Lighting cycles provide for 12-hour light/12-hour dark photoperiod in all housing areas. During the day photoperiod, dual lighting cycles are provided in all housing rooms to minimize retinal damage to albino animals. The only exception to the lighting cycle is a dark rearing mouse protocol (where animals are housed in the dark 24 hours per day for 7 days per week) and the dark adaptation chamber which houses rodents under dark conditions for a limited period of time (less than 16 hours) in order to perform ERGs. Dark adaptation is an exception to The Guide and must be scientifically justified and approved by IACUC. Housing rooms do not have windows, with the exception of the Satellite Room (which has a window, but it is sealed with a double layered darkening heavy duty poly curtain). Although our housing room doors have view panels for safety, these panels are covered with a red film that maintains the animal dark cycle even when the hallway lights remain on after hours.
6.1.6. Cleaning and Sanitation

All rodent static cage bottoms are sanitized twice per week (static cages with two or less mice are changed 1/week). All rodent ventilated cage bottoms are changed every 2 weeks. Accessories are sanitized at least weekly. Rodent racks for static cages are cleaned monthly. Rodent racks for ventilated cages are cleaned in the room every six months. Washing and sanitation of caging equipment and accessories is processed in the rack washers. These units are monitored using temperature tapes daily to assure that 180ºF temperature is achieved by the end of the washing cycles. CHARMS bioluminescence swabs are also used to verify sanitation quarterly unless there are issues with the rack washers reaching 180ºF. The two rack washers will not complete a cycle and alarm if 180ºF is not reached. Soiled bedding is emptied within a HEPA filtered dump station in the dirty side of the cage wash area.
6.1.7. Body Weights

Animals were weighed at the start of the study and at 1, 3, and 6 months post-dosing during in vivo measurements, with a final measurement at the time of euthanasia. Animal body weights were recorded on the mouse cage cards and in electronic notebooks. Weights were compared to Jax published expected weight/week of age for C57BL/6J animals (https://www.jax.org/jax- mice-and-services/strain-data-sheet-pages/body-weight-chart-000664).
6.1.8. Quarantine
Mice were bred at SERI and therefore did not require quarantine.
6.1.9. Assignment to Groups
Suitable animals were randomly assigned to groups based upon body weight, and the procedure was documented in the study notebooks.
Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study in Rho Mice Report, v.02 Date of Report: 30 November 2021
6.1.10. Moribundity and Mortality Observations

During the study, all animals were observed by Haider lab staff members and animal facility staff twice per day on weekdays and at least once on weekends and holidays for mortality or evidence of moribundity, and any abnormal clinical signs were recorded. Each mouse was weighed and evaluated during dosing for general appearance as well as overt signs of toxicity, and any abnormal clinical signs were noted. Animals were euthanized immediately if the following signs were observed: eyelids partially closed, change in respiration, rough coat hair, increased vibrissae movements, unusually aggressive behavior, writhing, scratching, biting, self- mutilation, and hunched posture.
6.1.10.1. Moribund Animals

During the moribundity/mortality observations, any animal judged not likely to survive until the next scheduled observation period were, upon consent of the Study Director and/or Veterinarian, be removed from the study, euthanized, and necropsied. A body weight and appropriate tissues as outlined in this report were collected. These animals were recorded as being euthanized in extremis. During the treatment period, dead animals were removed immediately and necropsied, and the death data was recorded in the study notebook. Criteria for early euthanasia include intractable dehydration and lethargy, and animals were euthanized immediately.
6.2. Clinical Observations

Mouse fundus was examined by indirect ophthalmoscopy (IO). The procedure involves dilating the mouse eye with 1% tropicamide (which was administered as a single topical drop to each eye). Fundus examination was performed using a Keeler Ophthalmoscope with a 60 diopter lens.
6.3. Dosage Preparation

Test articles were provided by the Sponsor to the Haider lab at Schepens Eye Research Institute (SERI). The syringe used by the Haider lab for pre-IND studies is the Hamilton calibrated syringe. These syringes come pre-calibrated, and the Haider lab has Hamilton calibrate them annually. For manual dispenses, the syringes are accurate to within ±1% of nominal volume with a precision of 1% at 80% of the total volume (Hamilton Syringe Selection Guide). Compatibility of syringes and needle with OCU400 drug product was evaluated by determining the OCU400 drug titer following dispensing by a qualified qPCR method.
6.3.1. Basis for Dose Selection

Three doses are selected: 1 x 108, 1 × 109, and 4 × 109 vg/eye. Current studies showed that 1 × 109 vgc per eye is sufficient to provide a therapeutic effect. We chose one log lower dose to identify a lower limit and 4 × 109 vg/eye as a higher dose that falls within recently reported dose levels for toxicity.34,35
6.4. Test Article Administration

On the day of dose administration, animals were anesthetized with a ketamine/xylazine cocktail. Pupils were dilated using tropicamide (1% [w/v]) and cyclopentolate hydrochloride (1% [w/v]). To prepare syringes for injection, syringes were rinsed with deionized water followed by

Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study in Rho Mice Report, v.02 Date of Report: 30 November 2021

phosphate buffered saline (PBS). Exterior surfaces of the syringe barrel and needle were wiped with a lint-free tissue. Each syringe was cleaned after used with appropriate cleaning agent (Microcide SQ®) and rinsed again in deionized water and stored dry, in a sealed storage container. The eye to be injected was slightly proptosed by periocular pressure, and a 30-gauge needle was introduced into the subretinal space. A 33G 1/2" needle with a 10° to 12º bevel fitted to a Hamilton micro syringe was inserted, and 0.5 L of OCU400 was injected manually with consistent and steady motion into the subretinal space. 1% filter sterilized Fast Green dye was added to the diluent to ensure accuracy in location and delivered volume. This was proven to have no impact on the study and is included in the diluent-only control. Post-injection, a drop of ocular lubricant (GenTeal) and a small amount of AK-POLY-BAC antibiotic ointment (Akorn, Lake Forest, IL, USA) was applied to the eye. The mice were kept on a heating pad until waking. Forty-eight hours after injection, mice were macroscopically inspected, and those with any apparent ocular damage (e.g., cloudy eye) were not used for subsequent experiments (see Appendix for SOPs).
6.5. Device Compatibility

Device compatibility was performed at Ocugen by spike recovery analysis of OCU400 using the Hamilton syringe and a pipette. OCU400 was DNaseI treated, then diluted in TE buffer containing 0.001% PF-68 to the indicated dose levels (see Section 7.1) to assess recovery. Pre- dose concentration was measured from 5 uL in a pipette, and post-dose concentration was measured from 5 uL in a Hamilton syringe. Concentrations were then analyzed by qPCR.

This study was reported in the Ocugen/SERI Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study Report in rd7 mice, dated 22 October 2021.
6.6. In Vivo Analyses
6.6.1. Electroretinogram (ERG)

Diagnosis Espion ERG system was used to evaluate retinal function. Mice were anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine and xylazine diluted in sterile saline. Pupils were dilated with 2.5% phenylephrine and place on a temperature-regulated heating pad during ERG recording sessions. The conditions listed here are standard for eliciting ERG recordings to diagnostically test for retina function. GenTeal was used to lubricate the cornea. A DTL-type electrode was placed on the test eye. Silver needle electrodes, inserted under the skin of the bridge of the nose and tail, served as reference and ground, respectively. The ERG was amplified (10,000x), band-pass filtered from 0.1-1000 Hz, and digitized by a data acquisition board at 5000 samples/second. Typically 30 responses were averaged to reduce noise. Amplitude, morphology, and signal processing characteristics of the ERG were assessed offline using waveform analysis software.
6.6.1.1. Dark-Adapted Response

This procedure was performed in room 072 in the Diagnosis Espion ERG system at the Schepens animal facility following the guidelines found in the Animal Facility ERG SOP. Mice were dark- adapted overnight, then anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine and xylazine diluted in sterile saline. The ERG response was elicited by a 10 ms, 520 nm flash at an intensity of 0.38 cd s m-2 and responses to thirty flashes were averaged using a 1 second inter-stimulus interval (ISI). The

B-wave amplitude, measured from peak to trough of the waveform, was used as the response metric. Averaged data from experimental animals was plotted as a percentage of the average controls.
6.6.2. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy (IO) Imaging

Mouse fundus was imaged by indirect ophthalmoscopy using a Micron III (Phoenix Research) system, then examined by optical coherence tomography (OCT). Mice were anesthetized by ketamine and xylazine using a 0.5", 25G needle. Once anesthetized, mice pupils were dilated using a drop of 1% tropicamide followed by a drop of 1% cyclopentolate hydrochloride applied on the corneal surface. Eyes were kept moist by application of an ocular lubricant (GenTeal). For OCT examination, mice were restrained in a mounting tube fixed on a six-axis platform that was attached to the OCT camera. OCT scans were obtained once the mouse was properly aligned. Four rotational cross section scans (dorsal-ventral and nasal-caudal) with 100 series/scan were taken for each retina. Data were analyzed using Bioptigen OCT software.
6.7. Euthanasia

Animals were euthanized as quickly and painlessly as possible. Animals were left in their original cage, and a flow of CO2 gas was introduced into the cage. Following the inflow of CO2 into the cage, animals were observed to detect lack of respiration. Once the animal was observed as lacking respiration, CO2 flow was continued for a minimum of one more minute. Rodent was individually removed from the cage, and death was confirmed by asserting cardiac and respiratory arrest.
6.8. Post-Mortem
6.8.1. Necropsy
At necropsy, a thorough external and internal examination was performed, including body orifices and cranial, thoracic, and abdominal organs and tissues.
6.8.2. Preserved Tissues
Gross lesions were to be preserved, however none were observed.
6.8.3. Unscheduled Deaths

For all unscheduled deaths of animals, a comprehensive gross pathology and histopathology was performed on all tissues of the animal to determine the cause of death. Two animals died while restraining and during anesthesia.

1. At known time of death, a visual analysis of animal was documented in the raw data by one of three lab personnel to account for physical characteristics such as alopecia, dermatitis, open wounds, etc.

2. When possible, tissue will be collected immediately after known time of death and labeled with date of death as well as animal strain, ID number, virus administration time point, and confirmation of the type of tissue.

3. Tissue was processed for gross histological analysis.

6.9. Statistical Analysis

Statistics were limited to the calculation of means and standard deviations, wherever appropriate. Student's t-test was used to confirm statistical significance of differential expression with a P- value of <0.05. Power analysis-based statistics were conducted using the G*Power 3.1 software analysis, estimating our sample size required for each analysis and quantification, using means and standard deviation (SD) described in published work from others, to calculate the minimal number of animals for gene expression analysis and histology of each treatment in order to provide 90% power to detect a 30% difference at a significance level of 0.05.36
7. RESULTS
7.1. Device Compatibility

This study was reported in the Ocugen/SERI Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study Report in rd7 mice, dated 22 October 2021. The results presented here are the same as in the sister study and are the same data.

Device compatibility was analyzed at Ocugen for the Hamilton syringe. Results from all analyzed samples were within 15% between pre- and post-compatibility (Table 6). Since this is within the variability of the qPCR assay, this suggest there is no difference and that the device does not affect the dose concentration.

7.2. Animal Health

No gross pathological or toxic effects were noted in treated animals. Overall animal health was not impacted by OCU400 delivery. Mice were able to eat, drink, ambulate, and function as normal animals with no obvious or concerning issues for the duration of the study.
7.3. ERG Analysis

Scotopic B wave amplitude ERG was measured to record rod and cone photoreceptor function of control (B6) and RhoP23H mice. ERG analysis shows improvement of photoreceptor function in all three doses. Animals treated with OCU400 at one month show significant attenuation and even improvement of their retinal function compared to untreated animals (Figure 1).

blocks.text: 8. CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSION

Preliminary studies using three different doses of OCU400 to treat RhoP23H related retinal degeneration shows that each dose effectively improves retinal function as assessed after one month. This study evaluated 3 doses (1 x 108, 1 x 109, and 4 x 109), and positive outcomes from treatment is observed with all three doses, including resolution of white lesions apparent in fundus imaging and improved retinal function assessed by ERG at 1 month post-dosing. Furthermore, no gross pathological or toxic effects were observed in any treated animals. Importantly, treatment was administered to RhoP23H retinas that already had significant degeneration.

OCU400 treatment was administered at one month in RhoP23H mice, a time when they already have significant retinal disease, to capture effects of NR2E3 treatment on intermediate to later stage of disease. Consistent with our prior publications, RhoP23H mice treated with OCU400 indeed show clinical and functional improvement. This improvement was observed regardless of the dosage. Additionally, no gross abnormalities or evidence of toxicity were observed on the mice or in the treated or contralateral untreated eyes. Improved retinal function suggests that

Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study in Rho Mice Report, v.02 Date of Report: 30 November 2021

OCU400 not only can attenuate but remarkably can reverse the degeneration process in a mutation agnostic manner. Additional dosing and further characterization by histology, immunohistochemistry, and longitudinal studies are underway.

12.1. SOP - Training for Technical Personnel and Eliminating Study Bias
container_path: 12.1. SOP - Training for Technical Personnel and Eliminating Study Bias

blocks.text:
1. All technical personnel performing subretinal injections in mice will be adequately trained by Dr. Haider (over 20 years' experience), or Dr. Datta (5+ years' experience), or animal facility staff.

2. All instances of dosage changes will be properly documented in lab notebooks (hard and electronic copies) and available for analysis throughout the study, as well as included in the final report.

3. To minimize any potential study bias, study implementation will include:

blocks.text:
a. Each litter will be randomly assigned to a dose and sacrifice time point to ensure no animal bias in study groups.

b. Our prior studies show no gender bias thus females and males will be used equally.

c. All three doses will be staggered at different points to eliminate a potential time bias. The first dose will be given to the first litter of pups, followed by the second dose administered to the second litter of pups, and so on to ensure a staggered schedule of administration.

d. A masked assessment of study parameters will be upheld via three personnel. One laboratory technician will be blind for the assessment of study parameters for each time point/dose. This system will operate in a rotational manner throughout the study to eliminate personal bias.

e. Fundus imaging via micron, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and electroretinogram (ERG), test will be utilized for each mouse at each time point/dose by the indicated masked personnel to assess effectiveness of AAV5-hNR2E32. B6 age-matched controls and RhoP23H animals with no injection, mock injection, and diluent (formulation buffer) = will be assessed as a control comparison to experimental animals.

f. Study director (Dr. Haider) will supervise the entire study and maintain all reports and will de-identify animals once all assessments have been recorded.

container_path: 12.2. SOP for disinfection and cleaning of Hamilton syringe and needles

1. Disassemble the syringe

2. Clean the syringe with an appropriate solvent or cleaning agent (Microcide SQ®). Following the use of a cleaning agent, rinse the syringe with deionized water and finally acetone.

3. Wipe the exterior surfaces of the syringe barrel and needle with a lint-free tissue. Make sure that there is no residual cleaning agent in the syringe before using or storing the syringe.

blocks.text: 12.3. Protocol for subretinal injection in adult mice
container_path: 12.3. Protocol for subretinal injection in adult mice

blocks.text: 1. Mouse will be anesthetized with a ketamine/xylazine cocktail (120 mg/kg, 16 mg/kg, respectively).
container_path: 12.3. Protocol for subretinal injection in adult mice

blocks.text:
Proof-of-Concept Dose Range Study in Rho Mice Report, v.02 Date of Report: 30 November 2021

2. Test eye will be slightly proposed by periocular pressure and a 30-gauge needle will be introduced into the vitreous cavity to make a hole in the subretinal space. A 33G 1/2" needle with a 10° to 12° bevel fitted to a Hamilton micro syringe will be inserted a ~45° angle and the needle tip will be directed into the subretinal space.

3. 0.5 microliters of OCU400 will be injected with consistent and steady motion into the vitreous or subretinal space.

4. Postinjection, a drop of GenTeal and a small amount of AK-POLY-BAC antibiotic ointment (Akorn, Lake Forest, IL, USA) were applied to the eye. The mice will be kept on heating pad until they wake up.

5. Forty-eight hours after injection, mice will be macroscopically inspected and those with any apparent ocular damage (e.g., cloudy eye) will not used for subsequent experiments.

blocks.text: 12.4. SOP - Unscheduled Deaths

For all unscheduled deaths of animals, a comprehensive gross pathology and histopathology will be performed on all tissues of the animal to determine the cause of death.

a. At known time of death, a visual analysis of animal will be documented in the raw data by one of three lab personnel to account for physical characteristics such as alopecia, dermatitis, open wounds, etc.

b. Tissue will be collected immediately after known time of death and labeled with date of death as well as animal strain, ID number, virus administration time point, and confirmation of the type of tissue.

c. Tissue will be processed for gross histological analysis.

d. Genome copy number of the vector will be assessed via real-time PCR as described in the Viral Titer and Exogenous Nr2e3 Expression SOP.
